questions.q: How do people usually judge what something is worth?
a: By comparing it with whatever is nearby
By calculating its cost of production
By recalling what they paid last time
By asking an expert for a valuation
questions.why: Lesson 1 says we are wired to compare, and we do it with whatever happens to be in front of us.

questions.q: Why does adding a slightly worse option help sell your product?
a: It gives buyers an easy comparison in your favor
It makes your price look negotiable
It signals that the product is in demand
It distracts buyers from checking reviews
questions.why: Lesson 1 says offering a nearby but weaker alternative leads people to pick you more often.

questions.q: In the chocolate study, what happened when the cheaper item became free?
a: Most people chose the free kiss over the discounted truffle
Most people still chose the higher quality truffle
People split evenly between the two chocolates
Most people bought both chocolates together
questions.why: Lesson 2 says cutting the kiss to zero made 90 percent choose it, though the price gap was unchanged.

questions.q: Why is free such a powerful price, according to the summary?
a: It removes any possible loss from the decision
It makes the product seem higher quality
It encourages people to buy in larger amounts
It makes buyers feel they owe a favor
questions.why: Lesson 2 explains that free means the downside is zero, and we strongly avoid losses.

We prefer free items over cheap ones
We copy the choices of people around us
